Recent field surveys have provided detailed morphometric data for spawning aggregations of Golani round herring, Etrumeus golanii, in the coastal waters of the Red Sea. The maximum standard length attained by adults in the sampled population was recorded at 20.8 centimeters [Li = 20.8 centimeters], a value consistent with the upper size range documented for this relatively small-bodied clupeid. Examination of gonadal development in the collected specimens indicated that puberty, as defined by the presence of mature gametes, was reached at a standard length of 14.5 centimeters [Lp = 14.5 centimeters]. This length at sexual maturation represents approximately seventy percent of the ultimate body length and suggests a life history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive investment, a pattern frequently observed in schooling forage fishes subject to intense predation pressure from piscivorous fish and seabirds. The length-mass relationship estimated from the survey data, conforming to the equation Wwi=0.00537*Li^3.13, yields an ultimate wet weight of 65.5 grams [Wwi = 65.5 grams] for individuals measuring 20.8 centimeters, indicating a modest adult body size that reflects the species position as a low-trophic-level planktivore.

Complementing the adult measurements, laboratory-based observations on embryonic and larval development have been conducted at a stable thermal regime of 15.6 °C [T = 15.6 °C] to establish key early-life benchmarks. At this temperature, the period from fertilization to eclosion, corresponding to the transition from an encapsulated pelagic egg to a free-living yolk-sac larva, required 30 days [ab = 30 days] at a temperature of 15.6 °C [T = 15.6 °C]. This developmental duration is characteristic of clupeiform fishes spawning in temperate to subtropical waters, where moderate temperatures extend the incubation period relative to tropical congeners. The newly hatched larvae are lecithotrophic and exhibit a wet weight at birth of 0.0014 grams [Wwb = 0.0014 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of 1.3 millimeters and the volumetric density approximation for teleost eggs. This minute initial mass imposes a substantial size-dependent mortality bottleneck during the pelagic larval phase, as the larvae must transition to exogenous feeding within a narrow window before their endogenous yolk reserves are fully depleted.

Under the same controlled thermal conditions maintained at 15.6 °C [T = 15.6 °C], comprehensive demographic data derived from both wild-caught otolith-based aging and captive rearing studies indicate that the maximum lifespan for Etrumeus golanii approaches 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days], a duration that positions the species as a relatively short-lived member of the family Dussumieriidae. Compared to the broader clupeiform average, which includes longer-lived genera such as Brevoortia and Alosa, the lifespan of Golani round herring is comparatively brief and aligns more closely with the rapid life-cycle turnover observed in tropical and subtropical sardine and anchovy populations. The short lifespan is accompanied by a high natural mortality rate, likely driven by the combination of intense pelagic predation pressure, the energetic demands of continuous foraging on zooplankton, and the metabolic costs incurred during extended spawning migrations along coastal shelf habitats.

Field sampling conducted over multiple spawning seasons has provided insight into the reproductive frequency of this iteroparous species. Gravid females collected during the peak spawning months were found to produce several discrete batches of eggs over the course of the reproductive period. Specifically, an individual female releases an average of 12,000 to 18,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 12,000 to 18,000 eggs per spawning event], with an estimated 3 to 4 such spawning events occurring annually [F_R_i = 3 to 4 such spawning events occurring annually]. This batch-spawning strategy maximizes the spatial and temporal distribution of offspring across variable feeding environments, increasing the likelihood that at least some cohorts encounter favorable planktonic conditions. The combined annual reproductive output of approximately 36,000 to 72,000 eggs per female per year underscores a high fecundity typical of small pelagic fishes that do not provide parental care and rely instead on numerical compensation for high egg and larval mortality.

The pelagic larval phase following yolk depletion is characterized by rapid somatic growth and a pronounced allometric shift in body shape as the larva transitions through the flexion and postflexion stages. During this period, the post-larval transformation culminates in larval metamorphosis, a process involving fin ray ossification and the onset of scale formation, which prepares the individual for the pelagic juvenile stage. First successful reproduction in wild populations has been documented at approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], coinciding with the onset of the first annual spawning season following the juvenile growth period. This early age at first reproduction, within the first year of life, is a critical component of the species' compensatory life history strategy, ensuring that at least a portion of the cohort reproduces before encountering the elevated mortality risks associated with overwintering periods and intensified predation pressure from pelagic piscivores such as tunas and mackerels.
